吴承恩: Wu Cheng'en (c. 1500?1582) was a Ming-dynasty writer traditionally credited with Journey to the West, an imaginative epic of pilgrimage, faith, and rebellion.
罗贯中: Luo Guanzhong (c. 1330?1400) is traditionally regarded as the author of Romance of the Three Kingdoms, whose vast panorama of war, strategy, and loyalty shaped the Chinese historical novel.
曹雪芹: Cao Xueqin (c. 1715?1763) drew on his own family's decline in Dream of the Red Chamber, a psychologically subtle masterpiece about love and the fall of an aristocratic Qing household.
褚人获: Chu Renhuo (1635?after 1705) was an early Qing scholar and novelist whose Romance of the Sui and Tang Dynasties blends history, legend, and court intrigue.
孙武: Sun Tzu, probably active in the fifth century BCE, is traditionally credited with The Art of War, whose teachings on deception, intelligence, and adaptability have influenced strategy worldwide.
老子: Laozi is the legendary sage credited with the Daodejing, a foundational Daoist text on the Way, virtue, non-action, and the return to simplicity.
孔子及其弟子: Confucius (551?479 BCE) and his disciples established an ethical tradition centered on learning, humaneness, and responsible government; their conversations are preserved in the Analects.
庄周: Zhuang Zhou (c. 369?286 BCE) was an influential Daoist thinker; the Zhuangzi uses parable, humor, and dream to explore freedom, change, and the limits of certain knowledge.
孟轲: Mencius (c. 372?289 BCE) developed Confucian thought by defending the innate goodness of human nature and the ruler's duty to govern humanely.
墨翟: Mozi (c. 470?391 BCE) taught impartial care, frugality, and opposition to aggressive war, offering a practical alternative to early Confucianism.
韩非: Han Fei (c. 280?233 BCE) systematized Legalist thought, presenting clear laws, administrative technique, and institutional authority as the foundations of a strong state.
列御寇: Lie Yukou is a possibly legendary Daoist sage credited with the Liezi, a lively collection of stories about naturalness, relativity, and spiritual freedom.
佚名: This catalog label covers works whose authorship is unknown or uncertain; their anonymous voices preserve traditions shaped across many generations.
刘安: Liu An (c. 179?122 BCE), king of Huainan and patron of scholars, oversaw the Huainanzi, an encyclopedic synthesis of Daoism, cosmology, and statecraft.
鬼谷子: Guiguzi is a semi-legendary thinker of the Warring States period associated with strategic diplomacy; the text bearing his name examines persuasion, psychology, and political tactics.
古籍: This attribution denotes no single author but ancient texts formed over centuries, as myths and traditions passed through unknown storytellers, scribes, and editors.
司马迁: Sima Qian (c. 145?86 BCE) wrote the Records of the Grand Historian, spanning three millennia and establishing the biographical model for later Chinese dynastic histories.
干宝: Gan Bao (d. 336) was an Eastern Jin historian who collected brief accounts of ghosts, marvels, and popular belief in In Search of the Supernatural.
鲁迅: Lu Xun (1881?1936), born Zhou Shuren, transformed modern Chinese literature through incisive social criticism; A Madman's Diary and The True Story of Ah Q became landmark works.
老舍: Lao She (1899?1966), born Shu Qingchun, was a Beijing novelist and playwright whose Rickshaw Boy portrays an ordinary man's crushed hopes with humor and compassion.
沈从文: Shen Congwen (1902?1988) drew inspiration from the cultures of western Hunan; his lucid, lyrical Border Town depicts human kindness and quiet tragedy in a rural world.
巴金: Ba Jin (1904?2005), born Li Yaotang, became a major May Fourth voice against patriarchal constraint through his Family and Love trilogies.
钱钟书: Qian Zhongshu (1910?1998) was an exceptionally learned scholar whose satirical novel Fortress Besieged wittily dissects marriage, ambition, and Chinese intellectual life in the 1940s.
张爱玲: Zhang Ailing (1920?1995), also known as Eileen Chang, portrayed love, betrayal, and women's survival in colonial Shanghai and wartime Hong Kong with exacting style.
圣埃克苏佩里: Antoine de Saint-Exup?ry (1900?1944) joined his experience as an aviator with philosophical storytelling; The Little Prince is a poetic fable of friendship, responsibility, and loss.
雨果: Victor Hugo (1802?1885), a leading French Romantic, combined epic storytelling with a commitment to social justice in Les Mis?rables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
大仲马: Alexandre Dumas (1802?1870) brought history alive through fast-paced serialized fiction; The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo celebrate adventure, loyalty, and retribution.
小仲马: Alexandre Dumas fils (1824?1895) examined social morality and women's position; his novel and play The Lady of the Camellias inspired Verdi's La traviata.
凡尔纳: Jules Verne (1828?1905) united scientific curiosity with adventure in novels such as Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas and Around the World in Eighty Days, helping shape modern science fiction.
福楼拜: Gustave Flaubert (1821?1880) pursued extraordinary stylistic precision; Madame Bovary uses free indirect discourse to expose romantic illusion and the confines of provincial society.
巴尔扎克: Honor? de Balzac (1799?1850) created in The Human Comedy a vast panorama of French society whose recurring characters embody money, ambition, and social ascent.
莫泊桑: Guy de Maupassant (1850?1893) was a master of the French short story who depicted war, class society, and human self-deception in concise, often ironic prose.
司汤达: Stendhal (1783?1842), born Henri Beyle, combined psychological analysis with social criticism; The Red and the Black follows ambition and hypocrisy in Restoration France.
卡夫卡: Franz Kafka (1883?1924), a German-language writer from Prague, transformed bureaucracy, guilt, and alienation into unsettling parables such as The Metamorphosis and The Trial.
歌德: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749?1832) shaped both Sturm und Drang and Weimar Classicism; Faust, his poetry, and his novels unite worldly experience with a restless search for knowledge.
赫尔曼·黑塞: Hermann Hesse (1877?1962), winner of the 1946 Nobel Prize in Literature, explored the individual's search for spiritual identity in Siddhartha, Demian, and Steppenwolf.
茨威格: Stefan Zweig (1881?1942) was an Austrian storyteller and biographer whose psychologically intense novellas and The World of Yesterday preserve the image of a vanished Europe.
席勒: Friedrich Schiller (1759?1805) was a dramatist, poet, and historian; plays such as The Robbers and William Tell join the desire for freedom with moral and political conflict.
托马斯·曼: Thomas Mann (1875?1955), winner of the 1929 Nobel Prize in Literature, examined bourgeois decline and the tensions of European modernity in Buddenbrooks, Death in Venice, and The Magic Mountain.
塞万提斯: Miguel de Cervantes (1547?1616) created in Don Quixote an early modern novel that parodies chivalric ideals while celebrating imagination, dignity, and the uncertain boundary between fiction and reality.
薄伽丘: Giovanni Boccaccio (1313?1375) framed the Decameron's hundred tales against the plague in Florence; its wit and realism opened new possibilities for European prose.
列夫·托尔斯泰: Leo Tolstoy (1828?1910) combined vast social panoramas with profound psychological insight in War and Peace and Anna Karenina, and later developed an influential ethic of nonviolence.
陀思妥耶夫斯基: Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821?1881) explored guilt, freedom, faith, and moral responsibility under extreme psychological pressure in Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.
果戈理: Nikolai Gogol (1809?1852) used grotesque humor and satire to expose bureaucracy and self-deception; The Government Inspector and Dead Souls profoundly shaped Russian prose.
普希金: Alexander Pushkin (1799?1837) transformed the Russian literary language; his lyric poetry, Eugene Onegin, and stories combine clarity, irony, and remarkable formal freedom.
屠格涅夫: Ivan Turgenev (1818?1883) portrayed serfdom, generational conflict, and the rise of Russian nihilism in the elegant prose of A Sportsman's Sketches and Fathers and Sons.
柯南·道尔: Arthur Conan Doyle (1859?1930) was a Scottish physician and the creator of Sherlock Holmes; sixty stories made observation and logical deduction hallmarks of modern detective fiction.
简·奥斯汀: Jane Austen (1775?1817) examined love, money, and social rank through irony and brilliant dialogue; Pride and Prejudice and Emma are enduring models of the novel of manners.
夏洛蒂·勃朗特: Charlotte Bront? (1816?1855) gave an independent heroine a passionate first-person voice in Jane Eyre, combining Gothic tension with criticism of gender, class, and dependence.
艾米莉·勃朗特: Emily Bront? (1818?1848) left one novel, the formally daring and dark Wuthering Heights, a story of destructive love, revenge, and the Yorkshire landscape.
莎士比亚: William Shakespeare (1564?1616) created tragedies, comedies, and histories of extraordinary linguistic and psychological depth, including Hamlet, Macbeth, and A Midsummer Night's Dream.
笛福: Daniel Defoe (c. 1660?1731), a journalist and novelist, gave Robinson Crusoe new realistic force through concrete details of everyday life and helped shape the English novel.
梭罗: Henry David Thoreau (1817?1862) joined an experiment in simple living with close observation of nature in Walden; his essay Civil Disobedience influenced nonviolent resistance worldwide.
菲茨杰拉德: F. Scott Fitzgerald (1896?1940) became the chronicler of the Jazz Age; The Great Gatsby turns wealth, self-invention, and the fragile American dream into an elegant tragedy.
海明威: Ernest Hemingway (1899?1961), winner of the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature, shaped a terse, suggestive prose style in works such as A Farewell to Arms and The Old Man and the Sea.
乔治·奥威尔: George Orwell (1903?1950), born Eric Blair, made Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four enduring warnings against totalitarianism, propaganda, and the political manipulation of language.
玛丽·雪莱: Mary Shelley (1797?1851) wrote Frankenstein as a young woman, creating a foundational work of science fiction about creative responsibility, isolation, and the ethical limits of scientific ambition.
王尔德: Oscar Wilde (1854?1900) combined sparkling wit with social criticism; The Picture of Dorian Gray and his comedies expose Victorian hypocrisy and the cult of appearances.
马克·吐温: Mark Twain (1835?1910), born Samuel Clemens, brought vernacular speech and satire into American literature; Adventures of Huckleberry Finn centers freedom and racism along the Mississippi.
梅尔维尔: Herman Melville (1819?1891) transformed his seafaring experience into Moby-Dick, a many-layered novel about obsession, labor, nature, and the limits of human knowledge.
杰克·伦敦: Jack London (1876?1916) drew on experience as a sailor and prospector; The Call of the Wild and White Fang examine survival, instinct, and the relationship between civilization and nature.
爱伦·坡: Edgar Allan Poe (1809?1849) pioneered the modern short story, detective fiction, and psychological horror; his precisely constructed works explore fear, loss, and obsession.
